name: Hameed
definition: Hameed is a composite portrait of a Muslim chilli trader in Kundgol taluk, Dharwad district, who built his business from a single tempo into a small fleet of three lorries hauling produce to Hubballi APMC and beyond. He embodies the trading networks, multilingual ease, credit pressures and educational aspirations that shape middle-tier agricultural commerce in the black-soil cotton and chilli belt of Kitturu Karnataka.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Hameed owns three Tata 407 lorries and trades chilli, cotton and jowar between Kundgol, Hubballi APMC and occasionally Byadgi market. His day begins at four-thirty with Fajr prayers at the neighbourhood mosque, followed by phone calls to commission agents and farmers about the day's rates. By six he is at the Kundgol market yard, inspecting heaps of dried chilli and negotiating prices per quintal with smallholders who know him by name. He arranges loading, drafts invoices and dispatches one lorry to Hubballi by eight. The other two run fixed routes to Gadag and Haveri, returning by evening. His income swings wildly: in a good month he clears thirty to forty thousand rupees after diesel, driver wages, toll and APMC fees, but when chilli prices crash—as they did in March 2024, falling from twenty thousand to eight thousand per quintal—he barely covers costs. He has taken loans from two commission agents and a Canara Bank overdraft of three lakh rupees, which he services by juggling payments and delaying repairs. His phone never stops; he speaks Kannada with farmers, Urdu with relatives and a mix of both with his drivers, one Hindu and two Muslim.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Hameed lives in a rented two-room house with a small courtyard in Kundgol town, sharing the compound with two other tenant families. His wife Ayesha, thirty-eight, manages the household and cooks for the family of six: their three sons aged nineteen, sixteen and twelve, and a daughter aged fourteen. His eldest son completed PU in Kannada medium at the Government Junior College in Kundgol and now helps with the lorry business, learning accounts and market talk. The second son is in tenth standard at the same college, preparing for SSLC, and Hameed insists he continue to PU and perhaps attempt a BCom. His daughter studies in ninth at the Government High School and Hameed wants her to finish at least SSLC, though his wife worries about the cost of private PU college if the government one has no Urdu option. His youngest son is in seventh. Ayesha's day revolves around meals, the children's homework and managing the ration card and Gruha Lakshmi payments, which arrived late three times this year. Hameed's mother, seventy, lives in their native village near Gadag and he sends her two thousand rupees monthly. Gender roles are traditional: Ayesha does not work outside, but she controls household savings and decides on children's clothes and school fees.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: He is determined his children will finish at least PU. His eldest completed PU in arts stream with sixty-two per cent, good enough for a BCom seat, but Hameed needs him in the business now and promised he can study part-time later. The second son, in tenth, travels five kilometres by bus to Kundgol for school; the annual cost—uniforms, books, fees, tuition for maths and science—comes to around twelve thousand rupees. Hameed pays another six thousand yearly for private tuition because the government high school classes are overcrowded and the boy struggles with English. His daughter attends the same school; she is a strong student, but there is no girls' hostel nearby and Hameed has heard that the Urdu-medium stream at PU level in Kundgol is weak, so he may send her to a private Kannada-medium college in Hubballi if he can afford the fifteen thousand rupees per year. His youngest son studies at the Urdu-medium primary school in the market ward. Hameed worries that his sons will not find stable jobs without degrees, yet he also sees educated boys from the neighbourhood driving autos or working shop counters. He wants at least one son to study BCom or ITI so the family has a government or bank job to fall back on when market swings hurt.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Hameed suffers from acid reflux and high blood pressure, diagnosed two years ago at a private clinic in Kundgol after chest pain scared him into a check-up. The doctor prescribed daily tablets—Telma and a statin—which cost four hundred and fifty rupees a month, but Hameed skips them when cash is tight. He smokes five to six beedis a day, a habit he knows he should quit. His wife has chronic joint pain and anaemia; a blood test at the government PHC in Kundgol showed low haemoglobin, and the ANM gave her iron tablets, but she says they upset her stomach. The children are mostly healthy, though his daughter missed school for a week last monsoon with dengue-like fever; they took her to a private doctor in Hubballi who charged two thousand rupees for tests and drips. Hameed knows serious illness means a trip to KIMS Hubballi or SDM Hospital in Dharwad, an hour away, and that scares him because one hospitalisation could wipe out his savings. He is enrolled in Ayushman Bharat through his ration card, but he has never used it and is not sure which hospitals accept it. Drinking water in Kundgol comes from borewells and an open tank; in summer it smells faintly of mud and everyone boils it. Heat exhaustion hits the lorry drivers in April and May; Hameed keeps ORS sachets and a first-aid box in each vehicle.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Hameed is Muslim, part of a Dakhni Urdu-speaking community in Kundgol that has lived here for generations, originally as traders and weavers. He prays five times a day at the Jama Masjid near the market, a modest whitewashed building that also runs a small maktab for Quranic education in the evenings; his youngest son attends twice a week. Ramzan and Eid are the year's anchors: the family fasts, the mosque organises communal iftar, and Hameed distributes zakat to poorer families and labourers. Relations between Muslims and Lingayats in Kundgol are mostly cordial; Hameed's business depends on Hindu farmers and agents, and he attends their functions when invited, though he declines food during Ramzan. The dargah of Shishunala Sharif in nearby Shiggaon draws both Hindu and Muslim pilgrims, and Hameed visits once a year for the urs, taking his sons along. His wife is more observant than he is, covering her head in public and insisting their daughter do the same after puberty. Hameed supports Congress because he feels BJP's local leaders favour Lingayat traders and sometimes speak harshly about Muslims, though he never discusses politics openly. He trusts the imam and a few older traders in the community, and they informally mediate disputes and pool funds for weddings or medical emergencies. He has no link to any NGO or formal SHG.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Hameed interacts with government mostly through the APMC and the RTO. He renews his lorries' permits and pays road tax yearly at the Hubballi RTO, a process that always involves a tout and costs more than the official rate. He holds a BPL ration card—upgraded to Antyodaya during COVID—and collects five kilos of rice and two of sugar monthly from the fair-price shop in Kundgol; the rice quality is poor but free, so his wife mixes it with market rice. His family receives Gruha Lakshmi—two thousand rupees monthly deposited in Ayesha's account—but it has been delayed three times in the past six months, forcing them to borrow from neighbours. Hameed has never claimed crop insurance because he is a trader, not a farmer, though many of the farmers he deals with complain they receive only a fraction of promised compensation after drought or hail. The local corporator is a Lingayat; Hameed went to him once to complain about garbage piling near the market, and the man listened politely but nothing was done. Hameed knows the Deputy Commissioner only as a name. He believes government schools are adequate for primary but weak in high school, and that the real benefits—pensions, Ayushman, Jal Jeevan—reach only those with political or caste connections.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Hameed is proud he built his business from nothing, and proud that his children will study further than he did. He worries constantly about debt: the overdraft, the dues to commission agents, the cost of one major lorry repair, and what happens if chilli or cotton prices collapse again. He fears one bad season or accident could force him to sell a lorry. He is proud of Kundgol's place in the Dharwad belt, the legacy of Sawai Gandharva, and the respect accorded to Urdu and Kannada both, though he quietly resents that Urdu-medium PU options are disappearing and that his daughter may have to study in Kannada or pay private fees. He blames middlemen and hoarders for price crashes, and blames the state for ignoring North Karnataka traders while favouring Bengaluru. He sees the Kittur Karnataka board demand as fair—Kalyana Karnataka got Article 371(J) funds, so why not Kundgol?—but doubts it will happen. He trusts the mosque, the dargah and old trader friends more than any government office. He is frustrated that educated Muslim boys struggle to find jobs outside teaching or small business, suspecting bias he cannot prove. He wants his children to have choices he did not: stable income, respect, and freedom from the daily grind of market swings and debt calls.
